newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec unveils plan to regulate gasoline prices.
newsitem.headline: Quebec unveils plan to regulate gasoline prices.

text.p: The government of Quebec said on Thursday it would present legislation giving it sweeping powers to regulate gasoline prices in the province.
Under the government plans, outlined by Quebec Energy Minister Guy Chevrette, gasoline retailers would be forced to charge prices at the pump using a minimum profit margin.
The move is being made after price wars, triggered by Ultramar Corp, over the past few months caused independent retailers to complain that their livelihoods were threatened.
The ruling Parti Quebecois government said in August, after prices fell to their lowest levels during this summer's price wars, that it was considering regulatory moves on gas prices.
Under the proposed legislation, a new agency, the Quebec Energy Board, would also be created to monitor and enforce prices.
"This series of measures have been adopted to permit sane competition in this sector, that has been at several times the scene of price wars," Chevrette told reporters.

He said the moves would mean major oil companies, which in Quebec also include Imperial Oil Ltd, Shell Canada Ltd and Petro-Canada, would be prohibited from posting prices at the pumps that were below those charged to independent retailers for resale.

"As a government, we have a duty to maintain the equilibrium between the interest of the consumers, who want to obtain prices as low as possible, and the survival of small independent retailers that create 10,000 jobs in Quebec," Chevrette said.
Gasoline prices, which have recently been around C$0.50 to C$0.60 a liter in most Canadian regions, dropped to as low as C$0.19 in the Montreal area in July.
